concepts.name: The machine finished. The artist’s goal is still unmet.
concepts.scene: A compact prop-packing machine has neatly delivered a crate to an empty inspection pedestal. Beside it, an artist holds a simple picture of the barrel they actually needed. The mechanism looks orderly; the mismatch between the requested object and delivered object carries the point.
concepts.job: Make the difference between completing an operation and completing the intended task visible in one glance.
concepts.edit: Keep the title, the UI/UX definitions, and the existing discussion question. Move the definitions into the left half. Place the illustration on the right; keep “A successful execution can still fail the task” as an editable line below it. No new slide.
concepts.layout: Landscape 4:3 cutout, right half of the slide, approximately 40% of the usable area. Make the requested barrel and delivered crate large enough to distinguish from the back of the room.
concepts.notes: This machine completed its operation. But compare what the artist asked for with what arrived. What would we need to inspect before calling the task successful? Think back to the renamer: a success count did not establish that the right objects changed.
concepts.rationale: This text-only slide is the conceptual pivot after the assessment. A deliberate visual mismatch gives students a concrete referent for the definitions without reproducing the assessment table.
concepts.limit: An illustrative analogy, not an engine failure or an argument that every UX problem is a functional bug. The caption and narration must connect it back to the actual assessment.
concepts.prompt: Create an isolated editorial teaching illustration: a simple compact mechanical prop-delivery device has delivered one wooden crate onto a small inspection pedestal. An adult environment artist beside it holds a large picture card clearly depicting a wooden barrel, looking thoughtfully between the card and the crate. Clear request/result mismatch, no exaggerated frustration, no readable interface, no lettering, no checkmark or success badge. Three-quarter view, only essential objects. Leave generous transparent margins. Match the approved Week 1 course reference in silhouette, restrained flat color, and dark navy outlines (#0A4054), with teal (#029990) as the main accent. Use modest natural wood and skin tones where needed. No glossy 3D, neon, glow, decorative gears, drop shadows, embedded labels or full-canvas fill. Export true RGBA transparency. The image is an illustrative teaching analogy, not a screenshot or documented result.

concepts.name: The revised prop, still in its scene
concepts.scene: An environment artist kneels beside a small game-environment diorama, comparing a revised lantern with its intended position beside a doorway. The light, doorway, nearby props, and camera remain visibly part of the scene. The illustration shows the artist’s desired outcome rather than a tool window.
concepts.job: Give “role, goal, benefit” an art-making context: the purpose of the import is to inspect the revised work where it belongs.
concepts.edit: Keep the title, all three user-story lines, and the existing success question. Put the illustration in the right 40% and reflow the story in the left 55%. If it crowds the benefit line, use the image only as a reveal after reading the story.
concepts.layout: Portrait or square transparent cutout; a single readable diorama, not a full fantasy landscape. The revised lantern should be the focal object.
concepts.notes: The artist wants to judge this revised prop in context. Importing is one step toward that goal. What should update, and what surrounding work should remain stable, so the artist can make that judgment?
concepts.rationale: The current slide names the benefit well but leaves it abstract. This picture reconnects tooling with artistic intent and the work students actually care about.
concepts.limit: Concept art of the desired workflow, not proof that reimport preserves lighting, placements, materials, or any particular engine state. Check actual behavior with the course demonstration.

concepts.name: Give them a goal; let them attempt it
concepts.scene: At a shared workstation, one student controls the mouse and studies the task. The tool author sits slightly back with a notebook, observing with both hands away from the controls. A small physical arrangement of three props and a lamp beside the workstation provides a concrete task cue.
concepts.job: Make the roles in an independent attempt visible before students start writing their peer-test task.
concepts.edit: Keep the title and all three preparation requirements. Add the small scene on the right. Replace only the bottom question with “What can your partner attempt without being told where to click?” Keep the four-minute writing block intact.
concepts.layout: Wide 3:2 cutout, two people, one workstation. Faces and posture should be readable; computer display angled away with no generated application interface.
concepts.notes: Give your partner an observable goal and a starting state. Let them attempt it before you explain the clicks. Notice where they hesitate and what they expect. If you provide help, record it. What will your partner be able to attempt independently?
concepts.rationale: The current text provides good task requirements. A human scene adds the behavioral expectation that is easy to forget when students are eager to explain their own tools.
concepts.limit: A fictional classroom illustration. Keep the real testing photo and role diagram on slides 45–46. Use this scene once; do not add another explanation or take time from task writing.

concepts.name: A visible boundary around the work
concepts.scene: A small prop workbench contains three crates inside a clear inset tray and a lamp outside it. An alignment jig reaches only the crates. The protected lamp is conspicuous and untouched.
concepts.job: Create a memorable image of bounded scope and protected surrounding work.
concepts.edit: Keep the existing fixture capture and code on this demonstration slide. Use this illustration only as an opening reveal if students need a scope analogy; remove it when the real preview appears. Do not shrink the evidence to fit a second visual.
concepts.layout: Wide 3:2 cutout with a strong tray boundary; shapes, position, and narration carry scope, not color alone.
concepts.notes: Before we run the operation, name what belongs inside its scope and what must stay unchanged. The tray is only an analogy. In the real tool we need to read the selected inputs, inspect the plan, and check protected objects afterward.
concepts.rationale: Useful if students confuse selection with everything visible. Lower priority because the existing fixture can teach this more directly.
concepts.limit: Do not imply that selection is a security boundary or that drawing a box enforces scope. Prefer an annotation of the actual selected objects when it is available.

concepts.name: The preview belongs to a particular input
concepts.scene: A work tray now contains two crates and a barrel, while a large earlier picture card beside it shows three crates. The same tray shape and viewing angle make the changed input easy to spot.
concepts.job: Show why a previously reviewed plan can become stale after an input changes.
concepts.edit: Keep this slide optional and preserve the existing precise process diagram. Use the analogy as an alternate opening image, followed by the current diagram. Keep slide 16’s backend code as the implementation reference.
concepts.layout: Two large objects in a 3:2 composition: current tray and earlier picture card. Add “Current input” and “Earlier preview” as editable PowerPoint labels, never generated lettering.
concepts.notes: Compare the picture with the tray. The picture may have been correct when it was made, but it no longer describes these inputs. What should the tool do before Apply? Rebuild the preview, then validate the reviewed plan again when applying.
concepts.rationale: A concrete mismatch can make stale state easier to understand than the phrase “invalidate the preview.” It complements the implementation explanation.
concepts.limit: The analogy does not teach concurrency or guarantee atomic execution. Do not imply that the current fixture provides broader transaction guarantees than its code establishes.
concepts.prompt: Create an isolated editorial teaching illustration with two clearly comparable objects. A shallow work tray contains exactly two wooden crates and one wooden barrel. Beside it stands a large paper picture card depicting the same tray from the same angle but containing exactly three wooden crates. Make the difference obvious. No arrows, text, labels, UI, clock, or extra props. Consistent three-quarter perspective and genuine alpha transparency. Match the approved Week 1 course reference in silhouette, restrained flat color, and dark navy outlines (#0A4054), with teal (#029990) as the main accent. concepts.name: Familiar craft, different workshop
concepts.scene: One artist carries a familiar small toolbox between two visibly different workbenches: a mesh-modeling bench and a scene-assembly bench. The person and toolbox stay consistent; the receiving apparatus differs.
concepts.job: Support the idea that general Python knowledge transfers while each host exposes different objects and operations.
concepts.edit: Keep this optional slide optional. Keep the title and three lines. Use the illustration on the right; retain host names as editable slide labels. Existing host icons are a simpler alternative.
concepts.layout: Wide transparent cutout, large toolbox, two simple workstations. Avoid bridges, robot mascots, product logos, and abstract cable tangles.
concepts.notes: You bring your Python concepts with you. What changes is the application you are working inside and the objects and operations it exposes. Which part of your Maya tool is a reusable rule, and which part talks directly to Maya?
concepts.rationale: A possible Week 1-style recall image, but lower value than the live-route concepts. The existing host icon family may do the job with less visual complexity.
concepts.limit: Not a claim that scripts run unchanged across hosts or that Python controls another application merely because it is installed.

concepts.name: Return to the four lenses
concepts.scene: Reuse the original four Week 1 badges beneath the existing synthesis content. Pair each with a short question grounded in the tool the student just tested.
concepts.job: Close the loop with Week 1 and give students familiar ways to explain their next revision.
concepts.edit: Keep the title and three synthesis instructions. Replace the small repeated test-loop thumbnail with the four original badges at a readable size. Add concise editable labels: Constraints · scope; Systems · dependencies; Leverage · reusable rule; Throughput · repeatable work. Keep the retest requirement.
concepts.layout: One horizontal strip, approximately 64–80 displayed pixels per badge in a 1280×720 layout. Use the original assets and names without recoloring or regenerating them.
concepts.notes: Which lens helps you explain the change you would make? What constrains it, what else is connected, what rule could help repeatedly, or what would make the work more reliable? Choose one consequential revision and tell us how you will retest it.
concepts.rationale: This is the strongest direct continuity with Week 1. It also avoids generating a new visual vocabulary when the course already has one.
concepts.limit: Use the lenses as discussion prompts, not a new grading rubric. Artistic intent remains the goal examined through the lenses, not a fifth badge.
concepts.prompt: No generation needed. Reuse the original course assets.
